     2	
     3	## Source
     4	https://www.sequoiacap.com/article/generative-ai-act-two/
     5	
     6	Published September 20, 2023 by Sonya Huang, Pat Grady and GPT-4 (Sequoia Capital)
     7	
     8	## The Foundation: Decades of Convergence
     9	
    10	Generative AI's emergence is not a sudden event but the culmination of decades of technological progress:
    11	
    12	- **Six decades of Moore's Law** delivered the compute horsepower to process exaflops of data.
    13	- **Four decades of the internet** (accelerated by COVID) produced trillions of tokens of training data.
    14	- **Two decades of mobile and cloud computing** put a supercomputer in every human's palm.
    15	
    16	ChatGPT's launch was the spark that ignited a Cambrian explosion of innovation not seen since the early internet. AI researchers became rockstars, hacker houses overflowed with autonomous agents and companionship chatbots, and the arXiv printing press became so prolific that researchers jokingly called for a pause on publications.
    17	
    18	But excitement quickly turned to hysteria. Every company became an "AI copilot." Inboxes filled with undifferentiated pitches for "AI Salesforce" and "AI Adobe." The $100M pre-product seed round returned. Cracks appeared: artists challenged machine-generated IP, Washington debated regulation, and a whisper spread that generative AI was not actually useful — products fell short of expectations with terrible user retention.
    19	
    20	## Early Commercial Traction Despite Skepticism
    21	
    22	Despite the discontent, generative AI has had a more successful commercial start than SaaS, with **>$1 billion in revenue from startups alone** — a milestone that took SaaS years, not months, to reach. Standout successes include:
    23	
    24	- **ChatGPT**: Fastest-growing application in history, with strong product-market fit among students and developers.
    25	- **Midjourney**: Reported hundreds of millions of dollars in revenue with a team of just 11 people.
    26	- **Character.ai**: Popularized AI entertainment and companionship; users spend an average of **2 hours per session** in-app.
    27	
    28	However, these successes don't change the reality that many AI companies lack product-market fit or sustainable competitive advantage.
    29	
    30	## The Retention Problem: AI-First Apps vs. Incumbents
    31	
    32	Mobile app retention data reveals a stark gap between established consumer apps and AI-first companies:
    33	
    34	### User Retention Comparison (Mobile Apps)
    35	
    36	| App | Category | Retention Rate |
    37	|---|---|---|
    38	| WhatsApp | Incumbent | 85% |
    39	| Instagram | Incumbent | 64% |
    40	| YouTube | Incumbent | 64% |
    41	| TikTok | Incumbent | 60% |
    42	| Snapchat | Incumbent | 51% |
    43	| Roblox | Incumbent | 41% |
    44	| Tinder | Incumbent | 34% |
    45	| Candy Crush | Incumbent | 32% |
    46	| Duolingo | Incumbent | 30% |
    47	| **Incumbent Median** | — | **51%** |
    48	| Character.ai | AI-First | 41% |
    49	| Runway | AI-First | 27% |
    50	| Remini | AI-First | 14% |
    51	| ChatGPT | AI-First | 14% |
    52	| Lensa | AI-First | 12% |
    53	| **AI-First Median** | — | **14%** |
    54	
    55	![Retention comparison: Incumbents vs AI-First Companies](./assets/figure_2.jpg)
    56	
    57	A separate monthly active usage benchmark for incumbents shows even higher engagement bars:
    58	
    59	| App | Monthly Active Usage |
    60	|---|---|
    61	| YouTube | 85% |
    62	| Instagram | 73% |
    63	| TikTok | 69% |
    64	| Snapchat | 67% |
    65	| WhatsApp | 63% |
    66	| Roblox | 61% |
    67	| Tinder | 54% |
    68	| Duolingo | 50% |
    69	| Candy Crush | 48% |
    70	| **Median** | **63%** |
    71	
    72	![Monthly active usage benchmarks for incumbents](./assets/figure_3.jpg)
    73	
    74	## From Act 1 to Act 2
    75	
    76	Sequoia frames the generative AI market as transitioning between two phases:
    77	
    78	**Act 1 (Technology-Out):** The discovery of foundation models as a new "hammer" led to a wave of novelty apps — lightweight demonstrations of cool technology. These apps used foundation models as the entire solution and often lacked stickiness.
    79	
    80	**Act 2 (Customer-Back):** The emerging phase focuses on solving human problems end-to-end. Key characteristics of Act 2 companies:
    81	
    82	- Use foundation models as **a piece** of a more comprehensive solution, not the entire product
    83	- Introduce **new editing interfaces** that make workflows stickier and outputs better
    84	- Are often **multi-modal** in nature
    85	- Solve problems **end-to-end** rather than offering thin wrappers
    86	
    87	Examples of Act 2 companies: **Harvey** (custom LLMs for elite law firms), **Glean** (crawling and indexing workspaces for relevant enterprise AI), **Character** and **Ava** (digital companions).
    88	
    89	The updated Sequoia generative AI market map is now organized **by use case rather than model modality**, reflecting the evolution from technology hammer to actual value delivery and the increasingly multi-modal nature of applications.
    90	
    91	## Key Findings
    92	
    93	- **Generative AI startups exceeded $1B in revenue faster than SaaS**, proving real commercial demand despite hype-cycle skepticism.
    94	- **AI-first apps face a severe retention gap**: 14% median retention vs. 51% for incumbent consumer apps — a 3.6x disadvantage.
    95	- **The market is shifting from Act 1 (technology-out) to Act 2 (customer-back)**, where foundation models become components of comprehensive, workflow-integrated solutions rather than standalone products.
    96	- **Multi-modal, end-to-end problem solving** and new editing interfaces are the hallmarks of companies likely to win in Act 2.
    97	- **Character.ai is the retention outlier** among AI-first apps at 41%, approaching incumbent levels, suggesting that companionship/entertainment may be generative AI's strongest consumer use case.

    16	> [!CAUTION]
    17	> ## 🚨 Global Execution Discipline (MANDATORY)
    18	>
    19	> **This workflow is a strict serial pipeline. The following rules have the highest priority — violating any one of them constitutes execution failure:**
    20	>
    21	> 1. **SERIAL EXECUTION** — Steps MUST be executed in order; the output of each step is the input for the next. Non-BLOCKING adjacent steps may proceed continuously once prerequisites are met, without waiting for the user to say "continue"
    22	> 2. **BLOCKING = CONFIRMATION POINT** — Steps marked ⛔ BLOCKING are confirmation checkpoints. If a user is present, pause and wait for confirmation.     23	> 3. **NO CROSS-PHASE BUNDLING** — Cross-phase bundling is FORBIDDEN.     24	> 4. **GATE BEFORE ENTRY** — Each Step has prerequisites (🚧 GATE) listed at the top; these MUST be verified before starting that Step
    25	> 5. **NO SPECULATIVE EXECUTION** — "Pre-preparing" content for subsequent Steps is FORBIDDEN (e.g., writing SVG code during the Strategist phase)

## 1. SVG Banned Features Blacklist

The following features are **absolutely forbidden** when generating SVGs — PPT export will break if any are used:

| Banned Feature | Description |
|----------------|-------------|
| `clipPath` | Clipping paths |
| `mask` | Masks |
| `<style>` | Embedded stylesheets |
| `class` | CSS selector attributes (`id` inside `<defs>` is a legitimate reference and is NOT banned) |
| External CSS | External stylesheet links |
| `<foreignObject>` | Embedded external content |
| `<symbol>` + `<use>` | Symbol reference reuse |
| `textPath` | Text along a path |
| `@font-face` | Custom font declarations |
| `<animate*>` / `<set>` | SVG animations |
| `<script>` / event attributes | Scripts and interactivity |
| `marker` / `marker-end` | Line endpoint markers |
| `<iframe>` | Embedded frames |

| Banned Syntax | Correct Alternative |

## 6. Shadow & Overlay Techniques

> `<mask>` elements and `<image opacity="...">` are banned. Always use stacked `<rect>` or gradient overlays instead (see §2).

### Shadow

#### Filter Soft Shadow — Recommended

Best for: cards, floating panels, elevated elements. `svg_to_shapes.py` automatically converts `feGaussianBlur` + `feOffset` into native PPTX `<a:outerShdw>`.

```xml
<defs>
  <filter id="softShadow" x="-15%" y="-15%" width="140%" height="140%">
    <feGaussianBlur in="SourceAlpha" stdDeviation="8"/>
    <feOffset dx="0" dy="4" result="offsetBlur"/>
    <feFlood flood-color="#000000" flood-opacity="0.08" result="shadowColor"/>
    <feComposite in="shadowColor" in2="offsetBlur" operator="in" result="shadow"/>
    <feMerge>
      <feMergeNode in="shadow"/>
      <feMergeNode in="SourceGraphic"/>
    </feMerge>
  </filter>
</defs>
<rect x="60" y="60" width="400" height="240" rx="12" fill="#FFFFFF" filter="url(#softShadow)"/>
```

Recommended parameters:
```
stdDeviation:   6–10     (smaller = crisper, larger = softer)
flood-opacity:  0.06–0.12  (keep low for a premium feel)
dy:             3–6      (vertical > horizontal for natural top-light)
dx:             0–2
```

#### Colored Shadow

Best for: accent buttons, brand-colored cards. Use the element's own color family instead of black.

```xml
<filter id="colorShadow" x="-15%" y="-15%" width="140%" height="140%">
  <feGaussianBlur in="SourceAlpha" stdDeviation="10"/>
  <feOffset dx="0" dy="6" result="offsetBlur"/>
  <feFlood flood-color="#1A73E8" flood-opacity="0.20" result="shadowColor"/>
  <feComposite in="shadowColor" in2="offsetBlur" operator="in" result="shadow"/>
  <feMerge>
    <feMergeNode in="shadow"/>
    <feMergeNode in="SourceGraphic"/>
  </feMerge>
</filter>
```

Replace `flood-color` with the element's brand color; keep `flood-opacity` between 0.12–0.20.

#### Layered Rect Shadow — High-Compatibility Fallback

Best for: maximum compatibility with older PowerPoint versions. Stack 2–3 semi-transparent rectangles behind the main card:

```xml
<!-- Shadow layers (back to front, largest offset first) -->
<rect x="68" y="72" width="400" height="240" rx="16" fill="#000000" fill-opacity="0.03"/>
<rect x="65" y="69" width="400" height="240" rx="14" fill="#000000" fill-opacity="0.05"/>
<rect x="62" y="66" width="400" height="240" rx="12" fill="#1A73E8" fill-opacity="0.04"/>
<!-- Main card -->
<rect x="60" y="60" width="400" height="240" rx="12" fill="#FFFFFF"/>
```

### Image Overlay

#### Linear Gradient Overlay — Most Common

Best for: image+text pages. Gradient direction should match text position (text on left → gradient darkens toward left).

```xml

<defs>
  <linearGradient id="imgOverlay" x1="0" y1="0" x2="1" y2="0">
    <stop offset="0%"   stop-color="#1A1A2E" stop-opacity="0.85"/>
    <stop offset="55%"  stop-color="#1A1A2E" stop-opacity="0.30"/>
    <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#1A1A2E" stop-opacity="0"/>
  </linearGradient>
</defs>
<rect x="0" y="0" width="1280" height="720" fill="url(#imgOverlay)"/>
```

Best for: cover slides and full-image pages with bottom title.

# Executor Consultant Top — Top-tier Consulting Style (MBB Level)

> Common guidelines: executor-base.md. Technical constraints: shared-standards.md.

---

## Role Definition

An MBB-level (McKinsey / Bain / BCG) top-tier consulting style SVG design executor. Suitable for strategic planning, board presentations, investment roadshows, C-suite decision support, and other **premium consulting** scenarios. Core characteristics: data-driven insights, pyramid-structured narrative, extreme simplicity. Output targets C-level decision-makers.

---

## SCQA Framework (Narrative Structure)

Every MBB-level presentation follows the SCQA narrative structure:

| Element | Purpose | Typical Pages |
|---------|---------|---------------|
| **S - Situation** | Establish shared context | Cover / Pages 1-2 |
| **C - Complication** | Introduce the problem / tension | Pages 2-3 |
| **Q - Question** | The implicit or explicit question to solve | Transition page |
| **A - Answer** | Core solution | All body pages |

**Page sequencing**: Cover embodies S+C → Executive Summary answers Q → Chapters develop A → Closing revisits S

**Title writing**:

| SCQA Element | Weak Title | MBB-level Title |
|-------------|------------|-----------------|
| S | "Industry Background" | "Digital penetration surpasses 60%, industry enters deep waters" |
| C | "Challenges Faced" | "Yet three structural contradictions constrain scaled deployment" |
| Q | "Strategic Question" | "How to move from pilot to full deployment within 18 months?" |
| A | "Solution" | "Three-phase path: Focus, Expand, Scale" |

---

## Data Contextualization (Never Present Data in Isolation)

> **Golden Rule**: Never display a single data point in isolation. Every number needs context.

| Method | Pattern | Visual Implementation |
|--------|---------|----------------------|
| **Time comparison** | "From X to Y" | Line chart + arrow annotating magnitude of change |
| **Benchmark** | "X vs industry average Y" | Bar chart with gray dashed baseline |
| **Competitive comparison** | "Us X vs Competitor Y" | Side-by-side bar chart, highlight own data |
| **Target gap** | "Actual X / Target Y" | Progress bar + gap annotation |
| **Ranking** | "Ranked #N of M" | Horizontal bar chart + highlight marker |

**Data annotation three essentials**: Every data visualization must include (1) The value itself (large bold font) (2) Comparison reference (baseline / prior period / competitor) (3) Meaning interpretation ("So what?")

```xml
<text x="160" y="280" text-anchor="middle" font-size="42" font-weight="bold" fill="#1E293B">97.3%</text>
<text x="160" y="310" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#64748B">Industry avg 82% | Competitor A 89%</text>
<text x="160" y="335" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#059669">Leading industry by 15.3 percentage points</text>
```

---

## Pyramid Principle (Conclusion First)

> Executives don't care about your *process* — they care about *results*.

```
         ┌─────────────────┐
         │  Core Conclusion │   ← Page title / Takeaway
         └────────┬────────┘
      ┌───────────┼───────────┐
  ┌───┴───┐  ┌───┴───┐  ┌───┴───┐
  │ Arg 1 │  │ Arg 2 │  │ Arg 3 │   ← Key supporting points
  └───────┘  └───────┘  └───────┘
```

| Level | Position | Font Size |
|-------|----------|-----------|
| Core conclusion | Takeaway Box | 16-18px bold |
| Arguments | Content area body | 14-16px |
| Supporting data | Charts / cards | 12-14px |

**Contrast**: Title "Market Research Results" (wrong) → "Metaverse needs 5-10 years to reach scale" (right); Body "We researched... and found..." (wrong) → "Three arguments: (1)... (2)... (3)..." (right)

---

### Content Page Standard Structure (1280x720)

```
┌──────────────────────────────────┐
│ Gradient top bar (0,0 → 1280,6)  │
├──────────────────────────────────┤
│ Assertion title (x=40, y=50, 24px)│
├──────────────────────────────────┤
│ Takeaway Box (x=40, y=75,        │  ← Dark background + white text, one-sentence conclusion
│   w=1200, h=45)                  │
├──────────────────────────────────┤
│ Content area (x=40, y=140,       │  ← Charts / data / analysis
│   w=1200, h=520)                 │
```

### Strategic Roadmap

Three phases laid out horizontally, `<rect rx="8">` + title + action list, `<polygon>` arrows connecting:

```
Focus Core (0-6mo)  ──>  Expand Capability (6-12mo)  ──>  Scale Up (12-18mo)
x=40,w=380              x=450,w=380                     x=860,w=380
```

### Benchmarking Matrix

Horizontal table; own row highlighted in theme color, others in gray. Leading indicators marked green, lagging marked red. Use `<circle>` or `<rect>` to build score points.

### Waterfall Chart (Change Attribution)

Start → increase/decrease factors → End. Positive factors green bars, negative factors red bars, start/end points dark bars, cumulative line as dashed connector.

---

## Strategic Use of Color

MBB-level color usage is extremely restrained — color serves information:

| Purpose | Method |
|---------|--------|
| **Focus** | Target data in theme color, everything else gray |
| **Reduce cognitive load** | Same series differentiated by opacity (`fill-opacity` 1.0/0.6/0.3) |
| **Semantics** | Green = positive, Red = negative, Gray = baseline |
| **Branding** | Gradient top bar / decorative lines in brand color |

**Commandments**: No more than 3 primary colors; accent color used at most 2-3 places globally; data series use same-hue depth variations, not different colors; background white or very light gray.

---

## Chart vs Table Selection Matrix

| Scenario | Recommended Form | Reason |
|----------|-----------------|--------|
| Comparing 2-7 categories | **Bar chart** | Visual comparison is intuitive |
| Time trends | **Line chart** | Time series clarity |
| Precise values / large rankings | **Table** | 50 data points in a bar chart would be chaotic |
| Proportional composition | **Donut chart** | More modern than pie charts |
| Two-dimensional positioning | **2x2 matrix** | Strategic quadrant analysis |
| Change attribution | **Waterfall chart** | Factor decomposition |

## Speaker Notes Style

### Narrative Tone

Targeting **executives / decision-makers**. Pyramid structure — every sentence carries information. Composed, authoritative, and insightful tone.

### Stage Direction Markers

| Marker | Purpose | Example |
|--------|---------|---------|
| `[Pause]` | Silence after key insight, let executives absorb | "This means we are missing a billion-dollar market. [Pause]" |
| `[Scan Room]` | Observe decision-makers' reactions, decide whether to elaborate | "[Scan Room] If there are questions, I can elaborate." |
| `[Data]` | Conversational number delivery | "[Data] 63% → nearly two-thirds" |
| `[Benchmark]` | Emphasize comparison baseline | "[Benchmark] Compared to the industry average of 12%, our 23% is nearly double" |
| `[Transition]` | Bridge from previous page, at start of each page's text | "[Transition] Building on the strategic framework, let's drill into the implementation path." |

### Notes Writing Guidelines

- **Pyramid structure**: Conclusion → Arguments → Details
- **Data contextualization**: Every number has a comparison reference
- **Executive language**: "The strategic implication is...", "The core insight is..."
- **Flex mechanism**: Annotate "content that can be skipped if time is tight" for flexible duration
- **Key points structure**: `Key points: (1) Core insight (2) Data support (3) Strategic implication`

### Notes Example

```markdown
# 03_strategic_path

[Transition] Having clarified the problem and the opportunity, now comes the most critical part — our response path.

We recommend a three-phase strategy. [Pause]

Phase one: Focus. Over the next six months, concentrate resources on conquering the Eastern China market.
[Data] Eastern China contributes nearly two-thirds of industry growth, [Benchmark] yet our penetration rate is only half of Competitor A's. [Pause]

Phase two: Expand. Use Eastern China as a template, replicate to Southern and Northern China.
Phase three: Scale. Leverage a digital platform for nationwide coverage.

[Scan Room] The resource allocation for phase one is in the appendix — would you like me to walk through it now?

Key points: (1) Focus-Expand-Scale three-phase approach (2) Data-backed Eastern China priority (3) 18-month full deployment
Duration: 3 minutes
Flex: [If time is tight, skip phase two and three details and go straight to financial impact]
```

- **Title**: Six Decades of Technological Progress Converged to Enable Generative AI

- **Layout**: Left-right split (5:5), two-column comparison
- **Title**: Act 1 Was Technology-Out; Act 2 Is Customer-Back

    - Novelty demos and lightweight wrappers
    - Poor user retention
    - "AI hammer" looking for nails
  - **Act 2 (Customer-Back)**:

    - New editing interfaces, stickier workflows
    - Multi-modal by nature

arguments.content:
# 01_cover

Welcome to our analysis of Sequoia Capital's landmark September 2023 essay, "Generative AI's Act Two." This deck examines how the generative AI market is transitioning from technology-driven novelty to customer-backed value creation — and what that means for investors and founders. [Pause]

The central thesis is simple but profound: Act 1 was about discovering the "hammer" of foundation models. Act 2 is about finding the nails that actually matter to human beings.

Key points: (1) Sequoia Capital's authoritative framework for understanding GenAI evolution (2) Data-driven analysis of retention gaps and commercial traction (3) Actionable takeaways for builders and investors
Duration: 1 minute

---

# 02_decades_of_convergence

[Transition] Before we diagnose where generative AI is going, let's understand where it came from. Generative AI did not emerge overnight.

The convergence of three massive technology waves created the conditions for this Cambrian explosion. [Data] Six decades of Moore's Law delivered the compute to process exaflops. Four decades of the internet — accelerated by COVID — produced trillions of tokens of training data. And two decades of mobile and cloud put a supercomputer in every palm. [Pause]

ChatGPT was the spark, but the fuel had been accumulating for generations. This matters because it tells us the infrastructure is real — the question is what we build on top of it.

Key points: (1) Three technology waves converged (2) Infrastructure is durable, not speculative (3) ChatGPT was a catalyst, not a cause
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 03_genai_outpaces_saas

[Transition] Despite the skepticism and hype-cycle noise, the commercial traction is undeniable. Generative AI has had a more successful commercial start than SaaS.

[Data] Startups alone have generated over $1 billion in revenue — a milestone that took SaaS years, not months, to reach. [Benchmark] ChatGPT became the fastest-growing application in history. Midjourney achieved hundreds of millions in revenue with a team of just 11 people. [Pause]

But here's the critical caveat: these headline successes don't change the reality that many AI companies lack product-market fit or sustainable competitive advantage. The $100M pre-product seed round returned. Inboxes filled with undifferentiated "AI Salesforce" pitches. [Scan Room]

Key points: (1) >$1B revenue proves real demand (2) ChatGPT and Midjourney are standout successes (3) Many AI companies still lack PMF
Duration: 2.5 minutes

---

# 04_retention_gap

[Transition] This brings us to the most important data in the entire analysis — and the core complication facing every AI-first company.

Look at these retention numbers. [Data] Incumbent consumer apps maintain a 51% median retention rate. WhatsApp leads at 85%. Even the lowest incumbent, Duolingo, holds 30%. [Benchmark] Now compare that to AI-first companies: the median is just 14%. [Pause]

That is a 3.6x disadvantage. Character.ai at 41% is the only outlier, approaching incumbent levels — and that suggests companionship and entertainment may be generative AI's strongest consumer use case. But for everyone else, this gap is existential.

Key points: (1) 51% incumbent median vs. 14% AI-first median (2) 3.6x retention disadvantage (3) Character.ai is the outlier at 41%
Duration: 2.5 minutes

---

# 05_incumbent_monthly_usage

[Transition] The retention gap is actually even worse than it first appears when we look at monthly active usage benchmarks.

Incumbents don't just retain users — they engage them deeply. [Data] YouTube leads at 85% monthly active usage. The median across all incumbents is 63%. [Benchmark] Compare that to the AI-first retention median of 14%. Even Candy Crush's 48% monthly usage exceeds the median retention of every AI-first app except Character.ai. [Pause]

This is the bar AI apps must clear. Retention is not a nice-to-have metric — it is the fundamental indicator of whether a product has found true product-market fit.

Key points: (1) 63% median monthly active usage for incumbents (2) Even lowest incumbent usage exceeds most AI retention (3) Retention = PMF signal
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 06_act1_vs_act2

[Transition] So what separates the companies that will close this gap? The answer lies in the transition from Act 1 to Act 2.

Act 1 was technology-out: foundation models were the entire product. These were novelty demos, lightweight wrappers, thin layers on top of GPT-4. They had poor retention because they solved no real problem. [Pause]

Act 2 is customer-back: foundation models are just a piece of a comprehensive solution. These companies introduce new editing interfaces, build multi-modal workflows, and solve problems end-to-end. [Benchmark] Harvey builds custom LLMs for elite law firms. Glean crawls and indexes workspaces for relevant enterprise AI. Character and Ava create digital companions that users actually return to.

Key points: (1) Act 1 = models as product, Act 2 = models as component (2) New interfaces and workflows create stickiness (3) Harvey, Glean, Character, Ava exemplify Act 2
Duration: 2.5 minutes

---

# 07_market_map_evolution

[Transition] This shift is so fundamental that Sequoia reorganized their entire generative AI market map to reflect it.

The old map was organized by model modality: text models, image models, code models. This was technology-first categorization — it focused on what the model does, not what the user needs. [Pause]

The new map is organized by use case: legal, enterprise search, companionship. It reflects the increasingly multi-modal nature of applications and the reality that foundation models have become components, not categories. [Benchmark] This reorganization mirrors the broader Act 1 to Act 2 transition: technology must serve the customer, not define the category.

Key points: (1) Old map: modality-first (2) New map: use-case-first (3) Reflects multi-modal reality and customer-back thinking
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 08_takeaways

[Transition] Let me leave you with five actionable takeaways for builders and investors evaluating generative AI opportunities.

First, retention is the critical challenge. A 14% median vs. 51% for incumbents is not sustainable. Second, foundation models must be a component, not the whole product. Thin wrappers will not survive. Third, multi-modal, workflow-integrated solutions will win — new editing interfaces create the stickiness that AI demos lack. [Pause]

Fourth, the $1B+ revenue milestone proves real demand exists despite hype cycles. The market is real. And fifth, companies solving end-to-end human problems will define Act 2. The question is no longer "Can AI do this?" It is: "Does this solve a real human problem end-to-end, with retention that rivals incumbents?" [Scan Room]

Key points: (1) Five actionable takeaways for builders and investors (2) Retention, component architecture, workflow integration (3) The bar is incumbent-level engagement
Duration: 2.5 minutes
